newsitem.title: UK: Clarke comments point to no UK rate rise - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Clarke comments point to no UK rate rise - analysts.

text.p: Comments from Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke that the strong pound was very anti -inflationary suggest it is highly unlikely an interest rate rise will be announced this morning, economists said.
"If anything it would suggest Clarke has decided to leave rates on hold," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr.
Clarke met Bank of Enlgand governor Eddie George for around 75 minutes on Wednesday afternoon.
Economists say the length of the meeting may have suggested disagreements between the two men.

"When that comment is taken with the fact the meeting went on for so long, it suggests the Bank was pushing for a rate rise and Clarke was resisting, using arguments such as the strength of sterling and the weakness of recent data to defer a rise," said Barr.

Wednesday's meeting came after the Bank's afternoon money market operations, so news of any change in official rates from their present 6.0 percent will come at Thursday's early operations around 0945 GMT.
Alex Garrard, an economist at UBS, agreed that the comments pointed to no change in rates.
"I would be most surprised in the light of these comments if they chose to raise rates," he said.

He singled out Clarke's remark that "When I make decisions on interest rates I look at how good were conditions in shops for Christmas, what is happening to production, how strong is the housing market getting...The big thing at the moment is the pound is very strong and that is very anti-inflationary."
Garrard said surveys suggested retailers had had a fairly poor December.

"We know that industrial production fell and we haven't had any major indications on the housing front," Garrard said. "Looking beyond the meeting, those are the three things that we'll get further information on."
Fourth quarter preliminary GDP figures on January 27 could be particularly significant in determining the outcome of the February 5 monetary meeting.
"It was the flash estimate of third quarter GDP that proved the major catalyst for the October rate rise," Garrard added.
